The orbital outpost was soaring 263 miles above the Indian Ocean, off the coast of Madagascar, at the time of this photograph. Credit: NASA. Date Created:2026-10-09

entries.title: Easy to integrate, compliant by design: Bringing the Swiss Franc to Google Cloud Universal Ledger
entries.summary: Every day, countless financial transactions are interrupted by slow, expensive, and inflexible conventional payment systems. As a result, public commercial stablecoins like Tether, USDC, and PayPal USD have become increasingly popular by making it easy to move money efficiently with instant, 24/7 blockchain settlement.Yet major regulated banks have largely kept such transactions at arm’s length; f
entries.content:
Nathaniel Zollinger

CTO, Crypto Finance Group

Moritz Platt

Capital Markets Technology Manager, Google Cloud

Every day, countless financial transactions are interrupted by slow, expensive, and inflexible conventional payment systems. As a result, public commercial stablecoins like Tether, USDC, and PayPal USD have become increasingly popular by making it easy to move money efficiently with instant, 24/7 blockchain settlement.

Yet major regulated banks have largely kept such transactions at arm’s length; for these financial institutions, reserve-backed public stablecoins present numerous risks, including strict capital and liquidity requirements and unmanageable regulatory and operational uncertainty.

Indeed, banks don't want to adopt existing stablecoins. Instead, they need the speed and efficiency of tokenized currency built on the trusted economic foundations they’ve nurtured over years or even decades in business. That’s why many are now turning to Google Cloud Universal Ledger (GCUL). Rather than channeling public stablecoins, GCUL provides the secure infrastructure banks need to issue and settle tokenized deposits. That brings real-time, 24/7 programmable payments into commercial bank money while satisfying regulators and without disrupting core banking operations.

For many banks, this is a compelling vision, but adopting new payment technology and integrating it with core banking systems can seem to bank CTOs like a daunting undertaking. That’s particularly true as they face mounting demands for the engineering resources that keep their businesses running while also striving to stay compliant with new regulations. But with a blockchain purpose-built for financial services like GCUL, this is anything but a herculean task.

Looking to expand its offerings for an increasingly global clientele, Switzerland’s Crypto Finance Group wanted to show it could deploy payment innovations like this in just weeks. That was its inspiration for launching a digital payments infrastructure pilot that enabled instant account-to-account transfers between customers of two Swiss banks on the GCUL network. The pilot, which was designed to operate within one of the world's most demanding financial security frameworks, provided a blueprint for how any commercial bank can build on Google Cloud technology to fundamentally modernize its payment operations.

Pain points in today's payments landscape

In recent years, there’s been a marked proliferation of tokenized payment methods. But stablecoins have transformed this previously niche technology, by effectively resolving some of traditional finance’s most enduring pain points, such as weekend transfer blackouts, direct transfers without correspondent banks, and fast settlement rails. Stablecoins also limit the frustrations caused by opaque cross-border transactions, where fragmented compliance checks can leave legitimate payments in extended and unexplained limbo and without a path to clear or timely resolution.

Still, commercial banks have been reluctant to offer popular reserve-backed stablecoins from permissionless blockchains to their customers despite their retail popularity. That’s because they come with numerous challenges to smooth and secure operations: an uncertain regulatory status, compliance issues around anonymous accounts, gas fees, and the scalability limitations of layer 1 blockchain technology. But perhaps banks’ biggest concerns about stablecoins is that they create a problematic economic disconnect — giving customers access to reserve-backed stablecoins reduces reserves and, as a recent McKinsey study found, banks’ ability to lend.

As a result, many banks are trying to figure out how to offer their customers the benefits of stablecoins — high speed, low cost, 24/7 availability, and programmability — without introducing problems often associated with existing reserve-backed stablecoins, such as regulatory issues, poor throughput performance, negative influence on bank reserves, and potentially no yield participation.

Solution proposal

Realizing this vision means modernized payments architectures must seamlessly and instantly enable individuals and institutions to transfer bank-held assets to accounts at any target bank. Orchestrating this shared ecosystem requires central entities to establish the governing rulebook, enforce issuance limits, and manage network-wide settlement parameters. During its pilot, Crypto Finance assumed this role, which within GCUL is known as the “currency operator.”

In this position, Crypto Finance can configure the network for either instant or deferred settlement. This choice is analogous to traditional banking: instant settlement acts like real-time gross settlement, where transactions settle individually and immediately and require high liquid reserves. In contrast, deferred settlement operates like netting, where payments are accumulated and offset and only periodically settle the net difference. For the pilot, Crypto Finance chose to adopt deferred settlement, in which GCUL manifests capital efficiency. In this way, clients enjoy instant transfers while banks conserve liquidity through periodic settlement.

Concept validation

To demonstrate instant, bi-directional account-to-account transfers on GCUL, Crypto Finance orchestrated a pilot with two digital token issuers, a Swiss digital asset bank, and a Swiss B2B transaction bank. Crypto Finance established the rulebook for interactions between the participant banks, such as interbank settlement, integration with traditional SIC payment rails, and AML/compliance protocols. Although some backend steps still needed manual intervention, Crypto Finance’s pilot proved that fully automated, cross-institution integration is feasible and established a generalized architecture that can scale to virtually any asset class.

Robustness and performance

A temporary pilot is one thing; moving into live client transactions carrying legal liability brings a whole new set of operational challenges. Live payment rails are considered critical infrastructure that demands security and availability. GCUL addresses these needs through redundancy between geographically distributed nodes operating on an enterprise-grade consensus model, ensuring reliability. Deploying client workloads on Google Cloud provides that enterprise-grade foundation and allows financial institutions to pair the highly resilient GCUL network with secure-by-design infrastructure, encryption at rest and in transit, and robust access controls that satisfy many of banks’ common regulatory, privacy, and data sovereignty mandates. While some banks may consider integrating their systems with fully public and permissionless blockchains, this approach introduces severe regulatory hurdles, anonymity risks, unpredictable gas fees, and low throughput. These are all roadblocks that in the past would have significantly delayed the pilot or rendered it a non-starter.

Ease of integration

The pilot's implementation, with systems integration completed in under three months, was compartmentalized across dedicated Google Cloud projects per participant. The currency operator, Crypto Finance, connected specialized components to a dedicated GCUL API. The first was a role admin service that controls account managers and token managers on the network. Next, it implemented a settlement registry to record when periodic off-ledger settlement between participant banks has occurred once a predefined threshold is reached. Finally, a cloud key management service (KMS) stored the currency operator keys to sign transactions.

At the same time, participant banks connected their core banking systems to their own GCUL API instances. But these participant banks don’t need a large Google Cloud footprint. Instead, they can connect to GCUL nodes via Remote Procedure Call from their existing on-premise deployments and manage private key material through solutions other than KMS. Regardless of the setup, transactions are seamlessly routed to the shared global GCUL nodes.

Whether GCUL is exposed to a bank’s client or used merely as a bank backend is entirely at the integrating institution’s discretion. The banks participating in the pilot chose the latter, utilizing the ledger to upgrade their backend infrastructure. With GCUL under the hood, they improved intra-day transaction performance and provided customers with the user experience they were already accustomed to.

Regulatory compliance and governance by design

To join the Swiss Franc currency network on GCUL, participants must have regulatory licenses that let them perform third-party transfers and issue commercial bank money. Crucially, features like token and account management are not rigid network-wide limitations. Instead, they rely entirely on the currency operator and its specific rulebook. This standardizes fees, limits, settlement times, and technical configurations.

Managing counterparty risk is central to this governance. Rather than relying on unscalable bilateral agreements or complex clearinghouse default waterfalls, GCUL mitigates risk through these currency operator-enforced issuance limits.

It’s important to distinguish GCUL’s broader feature set from the concrete pilot setup. In the pilot, both participating banks operated with conservative initial limits based on their credit ratings in order to safely prove the architecture. But beyond the pilot, the network frees up capital by periodically netting outstanding obligations, which frees banks from having to fund and settle every transaction.

Looking ahead, risk management can be further innovated. One clever future enhancement would be to allow participants to dynamically increase their issuance limits by committing digital assets as collateral in segregated accounts, using solutions like Crypto Finance’s AnchorNote pledging solution. These assets could then be used to instantly settle outstanding street-side obligations, virtually eliminating counterparty risk without tying up traditional liquidity reserves.

The future

While Crypto Finance’s pilot was designed to focus on domestic commercial bank money transfers in Switzerland, GCUL's programmable architecture and high-performance smart contract language, GCULpy, are paving the way for deeper innovation. As institutions like Crypto Finance scale their use of GCUL, the network can expand to support real-time cross-currency settlement, automated foreign exchange, and dynamic collateral management involving tokenized digital assets. And looking further ahead, this infrastructure has laid the groundwork for next-generation financial services that range from point-of-sale payments to autonomous, AI-driven agentic payments.

The pilot proved that deploying high-performance, blockchain-based payment rails doesn’t mean compromising on strict regulatory compliance or core banking stability. By combining the high-throughput of GCUL with a secure, API-driven integration architecture, commercial banks can offer stablecoin-like speed to their customers while seamlessly preserving their capital efficiency. Ultimately, this compliant-by-design approach targets the operational bottlenecks of traditional finance while mitigating the inherent risks and complexities of public blockchains.

To learn how your institution can build on this blueprint to fundamentally upgrade your operational payments infrastructure, contact Google Cloud Sales to explore the Google Cloud Universal Ledger.

The team would also like to thank Phil Dettwiler, Andras Miklos, Ignazio Pollina, and Ozan Kizildogan at Crypto Finance and Googlers Chris Esch, Ishan Singh, Olena Clayton, and Stathis Onasoglou for their contributions.

entries.title: Unifying enterprise context and semantics: LookML in Knowledge Catalog is now GA
entries.summary: As enterprises go from experimental AI agent prototypes to using them in production, data teams are realizing that access to data is not the same as understanding that data. To help bridge that gap, today, we are announcing the general availability (GA) of LookML semantic language indexing in Knowledge Catalog for Looker Core on Google Cloud.To answer a complex business question accurately, an AI
entries.content:
Maire Newton

Outbound Product Manager, Google Cloud

Ramanan Balakrishnan

Group Outbound Product Manager, Data Cloud

As enterprises go from experimental AI agent prototypes to using them in production, data teams are realizing that access to data is not the same as understanding that data. To help bridge that gap, today, we are announcing the general availability (GA) of LookML semantic language indexing in Knowledge Catalog for Looker Core on Google Cloud.

To answer a complex business question accurately, an AI agent needs context — table schemas, data lineage, governance policies, business definitions, etc.. However, context is not a monolith; knowing where data lives is very different from knowing how to calculate metrics with it. In the enterprise, teams often conflate broad organizational context (usually in the form of metadata from structured and unstructured documents) with deterministic business semantics (the exact SQL formulas, join paths, and filtering rules that define metrics like net revenue or churn), assuming that a single data catalog or a business intelligence (BI) tool handling both enterprise-wide asset discovery and precise metric calculation.

In reality, no one tool can carry the entire load for agentic AI, as enterprise agents require both organizational context and deterministic business semantics. In Google Cloud environments, those are provided by Knowledge Catalog and LookML:

  • Broad enterprise context with Knowledge Catalog: Agents need a unified context graph that aggregates metadata across structured tables and unstructured documents. Through Knowledge Catalog, agents discover assets, inspect data quality, trace end-to-end lineage, respect column-level privacy tags, and surface corporate policy documents. The context graph tells an agent what data exists, how it is governed, and how it is connected.
  • Deterministic mathematical semantics with LookML: What a catalog does not author on its own is how the numbers are computed. Describing a table is not the same as defining how tables join or how metrics are calculated. Looker's modeling language, LookML, encodes production-tested semantic logic — multi-grain join protections, conditional filters, and exact KPI formulas — so agents don't guess SQL math at runtime.

With this native integration, the LookML business logic that powers your trusted BI reporting is automatically indexed into Knowledge Catalog — giving Gemini Enterprise and custom AI agents both enterprise-wide discovery and deterministic BI semantics.

Why a context graph needs deterministic semantics

When an LLM agent connects directly to raw database tables — even when armed with basic table descriptions or a business glossary — it still has to infer mathematical relationships on the fly. Without explicit semantic rules, agents routinely fall into two traps:

  • Metric definition drift: Standard text-to-SQL agents can invent conflicting formulas for foundational KPIs like net revenue or customer acquisition cost, failing to apply domain-specific accounting rules (such as recognizing revenue only when order_status = 'Complete' or prorating annual contracts across active service days).
  • Naive join fan-outs: Complex schemas often contain one-to-many (1:N) and zero-to-many (0:N) relationships across invoices, line items, and refunds. Without pre-modeled join relationships and symmetric aggregation rules, agent-generated SQL can multiply rows and inflate financial totals.

Knowledge Catalog and Looker solve this together, enabling you to model once in LookML and access those semantics everywhere across Google Cloud's AI ecosystem. Knowledge Catalog enforces semantic math when that logic is defined in a semantic modeling tool; LookML provides a mature, production-proven language for defining those exact mathematical relationships.

What's new: LookML in Knowledge Catalog

Previously, catalog integrations only captured shallow, file-level pointers and basic dashboard inventories. With this release, LookML's deterministic semantics become a first-class layer in the Knowledge Catalog context graph. An agent that finds a metric in the graph now also finds its exact definition, its join path, and its lineage back to source tables — in the same place, under the same governance. Synchronization is always on by default with no action required from end users, and with live sync, any update pushed to production LookML is reflected in Knowledge Catalog in near-real-time so agents operate on the freshest business logic.

Because this metadata is indexed directly into Knowledge Catalog by default, it is immediately available to Gemini Enterprise, without custom agent code or separate catalog data stores. When connected to Knowledge Catalog, Gemini Enterprise uses built-in read-only skills and hybrid search to look up technical schemas, business glossaries, and indexed LookML logic in a single step, passing that rich context directly to your federated BigQuery connector to generate accurate SQL. (For developers building custom agents, the same context bundles are also accessible via the LookupContext API.)

Knowledge Catalog now captures and links the following entity levels across Looker Core on Google Cloud:

  • LookML models (looker-model): Captures descriptive metadata, database connection routing, include hierarchies, data validation tests (assert), and parent-child EntryLinks mapping models to their associated Explores, Views, and LookML dashboards.
  • LookML Explores (looker-explore): Indexes full relational join logic (type, sql_on, relationship cardinality such as many_to_one fan-out protection, foreign_key, required_joins, and sql_where) as Schema-Join relationships. It also captures mandatory filter guardrails (always_filter, access_filter), inherited dimensions and measures, and predefined starter queries that help agents and analysts overcome the cold-start problem.
  • LookML Views and fields (looker-view): Extracts column-level compiled LookML SQL expressions (for example, ${total_revenue} / NULLIF(${count}, 0)), primary keys, dimension group timeframes, field synonyms, and derived table transformation logic (including SQL and native derived tables, partition keys, and cluster keys).
  • Dashboards, Looks, and tiles (looker-dashboard, looker-dashboard-element, looker-look): Catalogs both UI-created and LookML-defined dashboards and visualization tiles, complete with dashboard filters, chart types, ownership, and usage statistics. Users in Knowledge Catalog are able to see table- and column-level lineage from underlying BigQuery tables all the way to individual dashboard tiles, allowing data engineers to evaluate schema changes proactively, before disruptions occur.

Looker Core on Google Cloud automatically indexes resolved LookML models, Explores, Views, lineage, and dashboards directly into Knowledge Catalog.

Three patterns for data agents

Bringing LookML into Knowledge Catalog gives Gemini Enterprise (and your broader agent ecosystem) a single place to retrieve both broad organizational context and governance from Knowledge Catalog and explicit mathematical relationships and SQL definitions authored in LookML.

To see the impact of combining these two layers in Gemini Enterprise, compare how three architectures handle a complex cross-domain prompt: "What was our total revenue last fiscal quarter by product category, and which regional promotional policy limits apply?"

When you follow pattern 3 and pair Knowledge Catalog with Looker's semantic layer in an enterprise agent workflow, the agent moves from guessing at raw SQL to a governed, two-stage execution flow:

  • Context and governance discovery in Knowledge Catalog: Before touching any data, the agent searches Knowledge Catalog, verifies that the thelook_ecommerce LookML model is gold-certified, checks column-level governance tags, and maps the prompt to exact LookML dimensions and measures, converting natural language into structured business intent.
  • Deterministic semantic execution: Rather than having the LLM invent SQL on the fly, the agent grounds its SQL in LookML's exact mathematical definitions indexed in Knowledge Catalog and returns trusted, repeatable figures.

Alongside the answer, the agent returns an interactive Open in Looker Explore link with the exact measures and filters pre-populated, letting users slice, dice, and inspect row-level line items in a single click.

Side-by-side comparison of a baseline agent querying BigQuery directly (left), which guesses at raw SQL and fiscal dates, versus an agent governed by Knowledge Catalog and Looker (right), which applies indexed LookML definitions and returns an interactive "Open in Looker Explore" link.

Scaling agents for BI and the enterprise

A common question from data leaders is: "If we use Looker Conversational Analytics, when do we use an enterprise agent grounded in Knowledge Catalog?"

The two experiences are designed for complementary jobs across your organization:

  • Looker Conversational Analytics is your dedicated BI assistant: When business users are working inside BI workflows and asking questions scoped to a focused set of curated Looker Explores, Conversational Analytics delivers immediate, self-service data exploration and visualization directly within Looker.
  • Knowledge Catalog + Looker powers your enterprise-wide agents: When users ask questions in Gemini Enterprise across federated Data Cloud sources like BigQuery, they often span structured tables, BI metrics, and unstructured documents. Enabling Knowledge Catalog in Gemini Enterprise gives the assistant built-in skills to dynamically discover relevant semantics across hundreds of LookML models, pass indexed LookML join definitions, metric SQL formulas, and starter queries to the BigQuery connector to prevent join hallucinations, and enforce centralized governance aspects and IAM.

Getting started

Because Looker Core on Google Cloud, Knowledge Catalog, and Gemini Enterprise are natively integrated, you can connect your existing LookML business logic to your enterprise AI assistant in just a few clicks, with no custom agent code required.

To start discovering Looker semantics and grounding your agents:

  • Confirm first-party metadata indexing is enabled for Looker Core on Google Cloud. This is enabled by default for new instances, with no additional charge for storing Looker technical metadata. Once enabled, metadata synchronization into Knowledge Catalog is always on by default (across both initial indexing and ongoing live updates). Enable the Cloud Dataplex API and Data Lineage API in your project and grant users the required view roles (roles/dataplex.viewer, roles/looker.schemaViewer, and roles/datalineage.viewer) to have your resolved LookML models, Explores, Views, join paths, and dashboards automatically sync into Knowledge Catalog.
  • Enable Knowledge Catalog in Gemini Enterprise. When you attach a BigQuery (or Spanner, Cloud SQL, or AlloyDB) data store in federated query mode to your Gemini Enterprise app, the Knowledge Catalog integration is enabled automatically. You can also turn it on or off at any time in the Google Cloud console by opening your Gemini Enterprise app, navigating to Configurations > Assistant, toggling on Enable Knowledge Catalog, and clicking Save and publish.
  • Ask questions. Gemini Enterprise connects to Knowledge Catalog using end-user credentials, meaning users only discover and query data assets they have IAM permission to view (such as roles/bigquery.dataViewer). Behind the scenes, the assistant automatically looks up your indexed LookML definitions, join logic, and starter queries in Knowledge Catalog and passes them to your federated connector to deliver accurate, governed answers.

To dive deeper, read the Manage Looker Core on Google Cloud with Knowledge Catalog documentation and learn how to Connect to Knowledge Catalog in Gemini Enterprise. To build a more customized experience, explore our hands-on ADK agent codelab on GitHub.

entries.title: Expanding Claude availability and deployment choice on Google Cloud
entries.summary: Every organization has unique requirements for building and scaling generative AI. At Google Cloud, we are committed to giving developers model choice and architectural flexibility to run workloads however they need. Today, we’re announcing the general availability of an Anthropic-managed deployment option for Claude Models on Google Cloud. This gives teams more choice in how they run their models
entries.content:
Michael Gerstenhaber

VP, Product Management, Gemini, Google Cloud

Every organization has unique requirements for building and scaling generative AI. At Google Cloud, we are committed to giving developers model choice and architectural flexibility to run workloads however they need.

Today, we’re announcing the general availability of an Anthropic-managed deployment option for Claude Models on Google Cloud. This gives teams more choice in how they run their models, helping them consolidate AI workloads on Google Cloud alongside our existingGoogle-managed deployment option.

Both options deliver the same frontier models on day zero, the same pricing, and the same Google Cloud billing. The difference comes down to who acts as your data processor and whether you need access to the new Claude platform features when they launch:

[NEW] Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed)

Delivers day-zero access to Claude models and Claude Platform features such as Claude Managed Agents (beta), skills, and code execution. Anthropic operates the stack as the data processor on Google Cloud infrastructure under Anthropic’s terms of service, while organizations authenticate with Google Cloud IAM, maintain Cloud Audit Logging, and consolidate spend under their existing Google Cloud billing and eligible commitments.

Learn more: Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic-managed).

Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed)

Continues to deliver day-zero access to the latest Claude models with strict governance, compliance, and sovereignty requirements. Google Cloud operates as the data processor under existing customer agreements, providing VPC Service Controls, Customer-Managed Encryption Keys (CMEK), and data residency in the U.S., EU, and APAC. New Claude Platform features roll out over time as they are integrated into the Google-managed infrastructure. Teams also benefit from native integrations with Google Cloud services like BigQuery and Model Armor, along with standard billing and eligible commitment drawdown.

Learn more: Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed)

Comparing deployment options

No matter how you choose to deploy, you can access Anthropic's latest frontier models on Google Cloud, including Claude Fable 5.1, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, and Opus 5.5, with new platform features available immediately on the Anthropic-managed option and rolling out on the Google-managed option once integrated. This gives developers the full spectrum of reasoning, coding, and multi-modal capabilities with Google Cloud IAM and Marketplace billing. Get started.
